text: A patient lies in a hospital bed waiting for hip replacement surgery.
In the patient's mind, the recovery is already done and the walking has already begun out the front
door. No cane, no pain. It feels wonderful. Yet in a well-known study, patients with the
brightest pictures of recovery were the ones their physical therapists rated as recovering worse
two weeks later. If you own a notebook full of plans you never started, that study may
explain why. And laziness is not the explanation. The psychologist behind it is Gabriele Urtingen
of New York University and the University of Hamburg. In 2002, she endorsed mayor, separated two
things most people treat as one. Expectation and fantasy. An expectation is a judgment.
Will this probably happen? You weigh your history, your skills, the odds. A fantasy is a scene.
Urtingen defines fantasies as the thoughts and images about the future that drift through
the mind's eye uninvited, in the shower, on a commute, or while staring at the ceiling.
The interview goes perfectly. The manager smiles, the offer arrives. Nothing in the
scene costs you effort. Urtingen and Meyer tracked both. Positive expectations predicted
more effort and better results. Positive fantasies predicted the reverse. Urtingen's
summary is blunt. These fantasies seduce you into feeling accomplished already and they drain your
energy. The pattern repeated in very different places. Students with the most glowing day
dreams about winning over a crush were less likely to end up with that person. Students
who pictured an upcoming exam going beautifully earned lower grades, while students who
simply judged they would probably pass, did better. Graduates with the rosiest visions
of their careers had a rougher start at work two years later and among the employed lower salaries.
None of this says dreaming is bad. Urtingen has said these fantasies grow out of real needs
and follow-up research found that people made to feel hunger or an urge to achieve
produced more of them. The trouble is that a daydream does not actually meet the need.
It only feels like it did. So what is the daydream costing you? Heather Kappas and
Urtingen answered with a blood pressure cuff. In 2011 they ran four experiments in which they
did not wait for fantasies to happen on their own. They assigned them. Some participants imagined a
desired future in glowing terms. Others imagined it critically, negatively, or neutrally.
Then the researchers measured energy. In one experiment women asked to imagine
looking and feeling great in high heels showed lower blood pressure than women who
thought critically about the same situation. Across the studies glowing fantasies left people
with less energy than critical negative or neutral ones. The drain was larger when
the need behind the dream was more pressing. The more you wanted it the more the daydream
cost you. In the author's words the same fantasy can leave a job seeker without the
energy to pound the pavement and a lovesick person without the energy to approach the one
they like. The author's explanation is that the mind moves into the finished achievement
early. The relaxation that normally follows real success arrives before any work has happened.
The body hears that the hard part is over which means every evening spent picturing
the finished business, the finished book, the finished body pays you a small salary of
satisfaction in advance. The salary is real. The work behind it is not that is the trade
these experiments point to. Pleasant and expensive but fantasy is only one way to get paid early.
There is a second way and you probably did it today.
In 2009 Peter Golvitzer and his colleagues published four experiments that opened
with an awkward question. What if announcing a goal makes you less likely to pursue it?
Participants held identity goals such as becoming a lawyer paired with a matching
behavior such as reading law journals regularly. When other people noticed that intention
participants acted on it less intensively than when nobody noticed. In real life they kept
striving less over one week. In the lab they jumped on fewer chances to act. The effect
appeared in people strongly committed to the identity not in weakly committed ones.
And in the final experiment being noticed gave people a premature sense of already being
the person they wanted to become. Attention filled a gap that only effort should fill.
These were short studies so treat the result as a risk not a rule.
But it explains why describing your dream to a friend can feel like a full day's work.
Underneath both traps sits something less comfortable. Big dreams come attached to
big tasks and big tasks bring fear. Fear of failing. Fear of finding out you are ordinary.
Fuchsia Siroas and Timothy Feigl argue that procrastination is less about managing time
than managing mood. Seigl puts it bluntly. Procrastination is an emotion regulation problem
not a time management problem. Their 2013 paper describes the pattern as putting short-term
mood repair ahead of long-term goals. A task makes you anxious so you reach for
whatever feels better right now. Scrolling, researching, rebuilding the same plan a fifth time
or sitting in the version of the dream that already worked. The finished version in your head
is far more comfortable than the blank page in front of you. Relief arrives now.
The bill goes to your future self. A meta analysis found that procrastinators lean
toward the present and away from the future partly because of their current negative moods
so the loop closes. The dream feels good. Telling people feels good. Starting feels bad.
And the brain picks the feeling. Dreading in's fix is not to dream less. It is to dream second.
Her method, mental contrasting, has two moves. Picture the wish and let yourself feel it.
And turn straight to reality and name what inside you blocks it. The tiredness.
The dread. The phone on the desk. Goal witzer supplies the next piece and if then plan.
If it is 7pm on a weekday then I open the document and write for 20 minutes.
The decision is made in advance so you do not need motivation when the moment arrives.
It works best when the plan serves a goal you truly want, not a weak one. Combined,
the two moves became whoop, wish, outcome, obstacle, plan. How strong is the evidence?
In 2006 review of 94 tests found that if then plans gave a medium to large boost to reaching
goals. A larger 2024 analysis, correcting for publication bias, estimated a smaller one.
A meta analysis of 21 studies on mental contrasting with if then plans found a small to moderate
benefit. Modest then but cheap and aimed at exactly this gap. Go back to the patient in
the hospital bed. Wanting to walk again is as human as wishes get. Nothing in the research
says that patient's mind was weak. It says a beautiful picture of the finish line can quietly
stand in for the road. So when a dream lights you up give it one minute and ask three questions.
What is in my way? What is my first move? And when exactly do I make it?
Write the answers down before the minute ends.
